sourceCourseTitle: Ai Governance Compliance Responsible Ai Leader / EU AI Act Readiness

body.en: In this lesson you will learn: 1) How the EU AI Act classifies AI systems by risk tiers (prohibited, high-risk, limited-risk, minimal-risk) and what each tier requires 2) How to determine whether your system falls under Annex II or Annex III high-risk categories, or is subject only to transparency duties 3) Practical steps to document classification, select the correct conformity assessment route, and prepare evidence for audit and market surveillance.

The EU AI Act applies a risk-based approach. Prohibited practices (e.g., social scoring by public authorities; untargeted scraping of facial images to build or expand facial recognition databases; manipulative systems that materially distort a person’s behavior and cause harm) are banned. High-risk systems include (a) AI safety components covered by sectoral product safety law in Annex II (e.g., medical devices, machinery, automotive) and (b) use-cases in Annex III (e.g., biometric identification; critical infrastructure; education and exams; employment and worker management; access to essential services like credit; law enforcement; migration/asylum; administration of justice). Limited-risk systems trigger transparency duties (e.g., informing users they are interacting with AI; disclosure for emotion recognition/biometric categorization; clear labeling of AI-generated or synthetic content). Minimal-risk systems (e.g., spam filters, AI in games) are largely unaffected but encouraged to follow voluntary codes. Classification hinges on the intended purpose defined by the provider. To classify: 1) define intended purpose and users, 2) check Annex II/III listings, 3) if not high-risk, check if transparency obligations apply, 4) otherwise treat as minimal-risk. High-risk providers must implement a quality and risk management system, data governance, technical documentation, logging, human oversight, and accuracy/robustness/cybersecurity controls, pass conformity assessment, affix CE marking, register in the EU database, and run post-market monitoring and incident reporting. Deployers of high-risk systems must use the system per instructions, perform data input checks, monitor performance, ensure human oversight, and keep logs.

• Intended purpose drives risk tier: map your AI to Annex II/III before assuming "limited" or "minimal".
• High-risk = life-cycle controls: QMS, risk management, data governance, documentation, human oversight, logging, conformity assessment, CE marking, and post-market monitoring.
• Transparency for limited-risk: inform users of AI interaction, disclose emotion/biometric categorization, and label deepfakes/synthetic media.

question.en: A bank deploys a customer-service chatbot that answers FAQs and routes users to human agents. How is it classified under the EU AI Act?

text.en: Prohibited AI practice
Limited-risk AI with transparency duties (inform users they are interacting with AI)
High-risk AI under Annex III (employment and worker management)
Minimal-risk with no obligations

explanation.en: General customer-service chatbots are typically limited-risk and require user disclosure that they are interacting with AI; they are not prohibited or high-risk by default.

question.en: A company uses an AI system to screen CVs and rank applicants for interviews. What is the likely classification?

text.en: Prohibited AI practice
Limited-risk with simple transparency only
High-risk under Annex III (employment and worker management) with provider/deployer obligations
Minimal-risk (no specific requirements)

explanation.en: AI for employment and worker management (e.g., recruitment screening) is listed in Annex III and is high-risk, triggering the full high-risk obligations.

question.en: A city authority scores citizens’ behavior to reward or penalize access to services. How is this treated?

text.en: Prohibited practice (social scoring by public authorities)
High-risk with conformity assessment
Limited-risk with disclosure
Minimal-risk

explanation.en: Social scoring by public authorities is prohibited under the EU AI Act.

body.en:
• Classification starts with intended purpose, then Annex II/III mapping.
• High-risk status triggers life-cycle requirements, conformity assessment, CE marking, and registration.
• Limited-risk systems require clear user disclosure and synthetic content labeling; minimal-risk are largely unaffected.
Congratulations! You have completed this lesson. You now understand how the EU AI Act’s risk-based model works and can classify AI systems and plan the appropriate compliance pathway.

title.en: AI literacy, transparency and GPAI obligations

body.en: In this lesson you will learn: 1) What the EU AI Act expects on AI literacy for providers, deployers, and affected personnel 2) When and how to meet transparency duties (AI interaction notices, emotion/biometric categorization notices, deepfake/synthetic content labeling) 3) Core obligations for general-purpose AI (GPAI) model providers, including documentation, copyright compliance, training data summaries, content provenance, and systemic risk controls.

AI literacy: The Act requires providers and deployers to ensure appropriate AI literacy of staff involved in the design, development, deployment, use, and oversight of AI systems. Organizations should provide role-based training, clear instructions for use, escalation paths, and records of competence; Member States and the Commission promote broader public AI literacy. Transparency: Users must be informed when they interact with an AI system (e.g., chatbots); natural persons must be notified when emotion recognition or biometric categorization is used; AI-generated or synthetically altered content (“deepfakes”) must be clearly labeled unless a lawful exception applies (e.g., for law enforcement or legitimate expression, provided safeguards are in place). GPAI obligations: Providers of GPAI models must prepare technical documentation for downstream providers; publish a sufficiently detailed summary of training data used (respecting trade secrets and confidentiality); put in place policies and technical measures to respect EU copyright (e.g., honoring text and data mining opt-outs and maintaining a data-use policy); implement reasonable cybersecurity and content provenance measures enabling detection of AI-generated content. GPAI models with systemic risk (very capable models meeting objective criteria) must additionally conduct and document model evaluations and adversarial testing/red-teaming, assess and mitigate systemic risks, monitor and report serious incidents, and cooperate with the EU AI Office.

• Build AI literacy by role: creators, approvers, users, and overseers need tailored training and clear instructions for use.
• Transparency triggers: AI interaction notices, emotion/biometric categorization notices, and deepfake/synthetic media labeling with clear, accessible disclosures.
• GPAI duties: baseline (docs, copyright compliance, training data summary, provenance) and, for systemic-risk GPAI, enhanced testing, risk mitigation, and incident reporting.

question.en: Your company rolls out a generative writing assistant to all employees. Which literacy step best aligns with the AI Act?

text.en: No training is needed because the tool is optional
Provide role-based training, clear instructions and oversight procedures, and keep records of staff competence
Train only the data science team; end-users can rely on common sense
Rely on a vendor disclaimer to cover all literacy obligations

explanation.en: The AI Act expects appropriate AI literacy for personnel involved in deploying and using AI, supported by role-based training, instructions for use, and oversight.

question.en: You plan to release a multimodal generative model trained on internet-scale data. Which obligations apply as a GPAI provider?

text.en: None until a regulator performs a market inspection
Only publish a marketing whitepaper; no need to support downstream providers

Provide technical documentation to downstream providers, publish a summary of training data, respect copyright opt-outs, implement content provenance, and (if systemic-risk) conduct evaluations/red-teaming and incident reporting
Register as high-risk and perform CE marking even if the model has no specific Annex III use

explanation.en: GPAI providers have baseline duties on documentation, copyright compliance, training data summaries, and provenance; additional testing and incident controls apply to systemic-risk GPAI.

question.en: A museum posts an AI-generated portrait on social media. To comply with transparency rules, what should it do?

text.en: Clearly label the image as AI-generated (synthetic) and, where feasible, preserve provenance signals
Do nothing because it is art
Hide the disclosure in website terms only
Disclose only if a user explicitly asks

explanation.en: Synthetic content (deepfakes/AI-generated media) should be clearly labeled for viewers; provenance measures help downstream detection.

body.en:
• AI literacy is an organizational duty: provide role-based training, instructions, and oversight.
• Transparency duties cover AI interaction notices, emotion/biometric categorization notices, and clear labeling of synthetic content.
• GPAI providers must document models, respect copyright, publish training data summaries, enable provenance, and, for systemic-risk models, apply strengthened testing and risk controls.
Congratulations! You have completed this lesson. You can now design AI literacy programs, implement transparency measures, and meet GPAI obligations under the EU AI Act.

In this lesson you will learn: 1) How the EU AI Act defines high-risk AI and the obligations that apply 2) The mandatory controls: risk management, data governance, technical documentation, logging, transparency, human oversight, and accuracy/robustness/cybersecurity 3) Practical steps to implement and evidence compliance, including quality management, conformity assessment, and post-market monitoring

Under the EU AI Act, high-risk AI systems (e.g., in creditworthiness, employment, essential services, education, migration, law enforcement, medical devices) must meet a comprehensive set of requirements before being placed on the market or put into service. Core obligations include: (1) Risk management system (Article 9): a documented, iterative process that identifies reasonably foreseeable risks across the lifecycle, defines risk acceptance criteria, tests mitigation measures, and feeds findings into post-market monitoring. (2) Data governance and data quality (Article 10): training, validation, and testing data must be relevant, representative, free of errors as far as possible, and complete for the intended purpose; with documented provenance, bias management, and gap analysis. (3) Technical documentation (Article 11 and Annex IV): a dossier describing the system, intended purpose, design and development process, data and model characteristics, performance metrics and limitations, risk controls, human oversight design, cybersecurity measures, and conformity assessment evidence. (4) Record keeping (Article 12): automatic logging to enable traceability, incident investigation, and monitoring proportional to risks and state of the art. (5) Transparency and provision of information to users (Article 13): clear instructions for use, system capabilities and limitations, expected accuracy, input data requirements, and human oversight instructions. (6) Human oversight (Article 14): design and procedures that enable trained persons to understand, appropriately monitor, override, or stop the system to prevent or minimize risks. (7) Accuracy, robustness, and cybersecurity (Article 15): defined performance targets, resilience to errors and attempts to manipulate the system, fallback plans, and secure development practices. Providers must implement a quality management system, undergo the applicable conformity assessment (often internal control or third-party assessment depending on the module and sectoral rules), affix CE marking, register high-risk systems in the EU database, and operate a post-market monitoring and serious incident reporting process.

• Risk management system: Continuous identification, analysis, testing, and mitigation of risks across the AI lifecycle, feeding into post-market monitoring.
• Data governance and quality: Controls to ensure relevant, representative, and sufficiently complete data; documented provenance, bias testing, and data handling.
• Accuracy, robustness, and cybersecurity: Defined performance thresholds, stress/adversarial testing, fallback/rollback plans, and secure-by-design controls.

question.en: Your team is building a credit scoring model (a high-risk use case). Which control is required before placing it on the EU market?

text.en: Publish the full model source code to ensure transparency.
Implement a documented, iterative risk management system covering testing, mitigation, and residual risk criteria.
Obtain explicit consent from all individuals whose data appears in any training dataset.
Rely solely on an internal code review by the development team.

explanation.en: High-risk systems must have a documented risk management system (Article 9) that iteratively tests and mitigates risks aligned to the intended purpose; the Act does not require publishing source code or universal consent for all training data.

question.en: To meet accuracy, robustness, and cybersecurity obligations, which approach is most appropriate?

text.en: Run a single accuracy test before deployment and accept the baseline results.
Ensure a human reviews every output, without any technical testing or monitoring.
Define target performance metrics, conduct stress/adversarial testing, monitor in production, and maintain a documented fallback plan.
Rely on vendor claims about model robustness without verification.

explanation.en: Article 15 requires defined accuracy targets, robustness testing (including foreseeable misuse), cybersecurity measures, and procedures such as monitoring and fallback to manage failures.

question.en: What must providers communicate to users of high-risk AI systems?

text.en: Clear instructions for use including intended purpose, input data requirements, performance and limitations, and human oversight measures.
Only high-level marketing materials describing benefits.
No information, to avoid confusing non-technical users.
All raw training data used to build the model.

explanation.en: Article 13 requires transparency and provision of instructions for use, including capabilities/limitations and oversight instructions; the Act does not mandate releasing all raw training data.

body.en:
• High-risk AI must comply with risk management, data governance, documentation, logging, transparency, human oversight, and accuracy/robustness/cybersecurity requirements.
• Providers need a quality management system, conformity assessment, CE marking, and post-market monitoring with incident reporting.
• Evidence of compliance should be built into development and operations, producing auditable artifacts aligned to Annex IV and Articles 9–15.
Congratulations! You have completed this lesson. You now understand the core high-risk requirements and how to apply them in practice.

In this lesson you will learn: 1) What technical documentation is required for high-risk AI under Annex IV 2) How logging and record-keeping enable traceability, investigation, and monitoring 3) How to design effective human oversight to prevent or minimize risks

Technical documentation (Article 11 and Annex IV) must provide a comprehensive, auditable description of the AI system and its lifecycle: intended purpose and system description; design specifications and development process; training/validation/testing data characteristics and governance measures; model architecture and configurations; performance metrics, evaluation procedures, and known limitations; risk management outcomes and mitigations; human oversight design and instructions; cybersecurity and robustness controls; post-market monitoring plan; versioning and change history; and conformity assessment evidence (including applicable harmonized standards). Documentation should be kept up to date and made available to competent authorities upon request. Record-keeping and logging (Article 12) require high-risk systems to automatically log events relevant to their operation, proportionate to the system’s context and risks. Typical logs include input and output records, model/version identifiers, timestamps, triggered thresholds, overrides, user actions, and error states. Logs must support traceability, incident analysis, and monitoring, and be stored securely with integrity protections and appropriate retention consistent with sectoral laws (e.g., data protection). Human oversight (Article 14) requires system design and procedures that enable natural persons to understand capabilities/limitations, detect anomalies, and effectively intervene—by disregarding, correcting, overriding, or stopping operation when needed. Oversight includes clear user interfaces, alerts/thresholds, interpretability aids proportional to risks, training for overseers, and organizational protocols that minimize automation bias and escalation delay.

• Technical documentation (Annex IV): A complete, current dossier covering purpose, data, model, performance, risks, oversight, cybersecurity, and conformity evidence.
• Logging and traceability (Article 12): Automated, tamper-resistant event logs capturing inputs/outputs, versions, timestamps, and interventions to enable audits and incident investigation.
• Human oversight (Article 14): Design and procedures that equip trained people to understand outputs, detect issues, and override or stop the system safely.

question.en: Which set of elements best reflects what must be included in high-risk AI technical documentation?

text.en: A marketing brochure and a brief accuracy figure.
Intended purpose, system description, data governance, model/training configuration, performance and limitations, risk controls, human oversight, cybersecurity, and post-market monitoring plan.
Only raw training data and source code.
A user manual without any development or testing details.

explanation.en: Annex IV requires a comprehensive dossier covering purpose, data, model, performance, risk management, oversight, robustness/cybersecurity, and monitoring—not just marketing, raw data, or a basic manual.

question.en: A hospital deploys a high-risk triage AI. Anomalous routing occurs. What logging approach best meets the Act’s record-keeping duty?

text.en: Disable logs to protect privacy and rely on memory recall by clinicians.
Log only final decisions, without timestamps or model version.
Automatically capture inputs/outputs, timestamps, model/version identifiers, thresholds/alerts, overrides and user actions, and error states, with integrity protection and governed retention.
Log everything indefinitely, including all personal data, without access controls.

explanation.en: Article 12 requires automated, proportionate logs enabling traceability and investigation, including key events and metadata, with security and appropriate retention aligned to applicable laws.

question.en: Which design best supports effective human oversight for high-risk AI?

text.en: Provide interpretable outputs, confidence indicators, alerts for abnormal conditions, clear override/stop functions, and training for operators to mitigate automation bias.
Hide system limitations to avoid alarming users.
Require users to accept all outputs to maintain consistency.
Allow overrides only by engineers, not frontline users.

explanation.en: Article 14 requires that trained natural persons can understand limitations and effectively intervene (disregard, correct, override, or stop) using clear UI controls and procedures.

body.en:
• Annex IV technical documentation must be complete, current, and auditable across purpose, data, model, performance, risks, and oversight.
• Logging must enable traceability and incident investigation with secure, proportionate, integrity-protected records and governed retention.
• Human oversight requires design and training that empower people to understand, monitor, and safely intervene in system operation.
Congratulations! You have completed this lesson. You now understand documentation, logging, and human oversight requirements and how to implement them.
